name: Oxyresveratrol

lead: Oxyresveratrol is a natural compound from mulberry and related plants, discussed as a skin-brightening ingredient for dark spots and uneven tone.

Tyrosinase is the enzyme that drives melanin production, and laboratory studies on mushroom and mouse melanoma tyrosinase report potent inhibition by oxyresveratrol, which is the basis for the brightening interest. Other lab and animal studies report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. No human trials of it for pigmentation or skin appearance were found.

paras: It is mentioned as an ingredient for brightening serums and creams. It is reported to be light sensitive and to degrade under UV exposure, so formulation matters.
No human safety data for skin use were found.

angle.text: Discussed as a brightener for dark spots and uneven tone. This mulberry-derived stilbene strongly inhibits tyrosinase in the lab, so less melanin forms. Studies so far are test-tube and animal work.

lead: Oxyresveratrol (2,3',4,5'-tetrahydroxystilbene) is a plant-derived stilbenoid, a close relative of resveratrol, found in mulberry (Morus) and jackfruit-family (Artocarpus) species among others.[1][2] For skin appearance, it matters because it inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that carries out rate-limiting steps of melanin production. Less melanin synthesis is the basis for its use as a skin-brightening ingredient aimed at a lighter, more even complexion.[3][4]

Most of the evidence comes from test-tube and cell work using mushroom tyrosinase and mouse melanoma cell enzymes.[3][4] A 2017 controlled clinical trial in Korean women tested a brightening cream that contained oxyresveratrol together with niacinamide, tranexamic acid, glutathione disulfide and linoleic acid, and reported lower melanin index and higher skin lightness after eight to twelve weeks.[5] Other laboratory and animal studies report antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects.[6][7][8]

paras: Oxyresveratrol is used as a skin-brightening ingredient in cosmetic formulations, usually alongside other agents. It is aimed at hyperpigmentation such as dark spots and uneven tone, the same target as arbutin and kojic acid. A 2022 systematic review of phytochemicals that inhibit melanin synthesis, covering 50 studies, lists it among compounds that reduced melanin in cell studies at 20 micromolar. The review notes that most findings come from cell or animal models and that oxyresveratrol was not among the agents confirmed in human trials.[9]

Oxyresveratrol is being studied in the laboratory for possible roles in stroke, Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, and for antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer and antimicrobial properties.[1][6][8][10]

Oxyresveratrol occurs in both gymnosperms and flowering plants. It has not been reported in plants of the subclass Sympetalae, a point the 2021 review calls chemotaxonomically interesting.[11] Among flowering plants it is concentrated in Artocarpus and Morus. It is the main compound in the heartwood of Artocarpus lakoocha, used in a traditional Thai remedy called Puag-Haad, and it is the aglycone of mulberroside A in white mulberry (Morus alba).[1][12]

A 1998 study found that oxyresveratrol from Morus alba inhibited the dopa oxidase activity of mushroom tyrosinase in a dose-dependent way, with 50 percent inhibition at roughly 1 micromolar.[3] A 2002 study compared oxyresveratrol and related hydroxystilbenes against mushroom tyrosinase and enzyme from murine B16 melanoma cells, reporting potent inhibition with an IC50 of about 1.2 micromolar on the mushroom enzyme.[4] Structure-activity work on constituents of Morus nigra roots has also examined tyrosinase inhibition by related compounds.[13]

The 2021 review describes unfavourable pharmacokinetic properties: low water solubility, poor oral availability and poor stability, which pose challenges to development and have prompted work on delivery systems.[11] In rats, adding piperine roughly doubled oral bioavailability, plasma peaks came 1 to 2 hours after oral dosing, the compound spread widely into organs, and oxyresveratrol glucuronide in urine was the main elimination route.[14]

Oxyresveratrol has been reported to scavenge free radicals more effectively than resveratrol in an assay using microglial cells,[6] to reduce inflammation in rat models,[7] and to protect neurons in rodent models of Parkinson-type toxicity and cerebral ischemia.[8][10] Phytochemical surveys list it among mulberry constituents.[2]

Oxyresveratrol is a tetrahydroxylated stilbene (formula C14H12O4) grouped with resveratrol and piceatannol. It is light sensitive and breaks down under UV exposure, and it is the aglycone of mulberroside A.[1] Crystal polymorphism has been studied by 3D electron diffraction.[15]

Controlled trial of a combination cream: a 2017 study in 26 Korean women who wanted to lighten their skin used a cream containing niacinamide, tranexamic acid, oxyresveratrol, glutathione disulfide and linoleic acid, applied to the face twice daily for 12 weeks, with photos at baseline and at 4, 8 and 12 weeks. Skin lightness (L*) rose by 0.7 at week 8 and 0.8 at week 12. Melanin index fell by 4.2 at week 8 and 3.8 at week 12. Erythema index improved at week 12, and more than 80 percent of participants were rated improved by both investigators and participants. The authors described the cream as effective and safe in Asian women. Because the cream contained five active ingredients, the study does not isolate oxyresveratrol's share of the effect.[5]
No human trial of oxyresveratrol as a single agent for skin appearance was found. Evidence on its own pigment-lowering effect is otherwise limited to enzyme, cell and animal research.[3][4][7][9]

No human safety data on oxyresveratrol alone were found. In laboratory work on Artocarpus lakoocha heartwood extract, oxyresveratrol damaged DNA in a dose-dependent manner but only in the presence of copper(II) ions, producing reactive oxygen species. The authors linked this pro-oxidant action to a possible anticancer effect.[12] A separate study reported DNA cleavage and apoptosis in Candida albicans.[16]
